meaning: Describes going through a feeling yourself, usually a strong and often unpleasant one, like “have a hard time” or “be embarrassed”.
connection: Adjective / な-adjective + な / noun + の / verb (modifying form) + 思いをする

senses.label: Experience a feeling
senses.meaning: You personally go through a certain feeling. The word before it is an emotion adjective, usually negative: 「つらい」, 「寂しい」, 「恥ずかしい」, 「怖い」. Positive feelings work too: 「いい思いをする」 (have a great time). It stresses “I actually lived through it” more than just saying 「つらかった」.
senses.connection: い-adjective + 思いをする / な-adjective + な + 思いをする (common: つらい・悔しい・恥ずかしい・怖い・寂しい・大変な・嫌な・いい)
examples: When I first went to study abroad, I couldn't make myself understood and felt very lonely.
I fell over in front of everyone and was so embarrassed.
I always have a bad experience at that shop, so I'm not going back.

senses.label: Make someone feel something
senses.meaning: The causative 「思いをさせる」 means making someone else go through a feeling. It is common in apologies and reflection: 「つらい思いをさせてごめん」. 「〜思いをさせられる」 means being made to go through it.
senses.connection: Adjective + 思いをさせる / 思いをさせられる
examples: I put my children through a hard time.
We sincerely apologize for causing you any discomfort.

notes: 「思い」 needs a modifier that says what the feeling is: ✕「思いをした」→ ○「悲しい思いをした」.
In an apology you mean “I made you go through ...”, so you need the causative: ○「不快な思いをさせてしまい、申し訳ございません」. ✕「不快な思いをして、すみません」 means “I felt unpleasant myself”, which reverses the direction entirely.
「〜思いをする」 means actually going through an experience (mostly a past event), while 「〜思いがする」 means a feeling wells up inside you: ✕「身の引き締まる思いをした」→ ○「身の引き締まる思いがした」.
Besides “enjoy a perk”, saying 「一人だけいい思いをしている」 about someone else often carries a sarcastic sense of “getting off easy / profiting at others' expense”, so be careful when talking about other people.

daily.title: Looking back
daily.description: Talking with a friend about hard times in the past.
daily.example: I had no money as a student, so I really had a rough time.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Your friend did badly on an exam, and you show you understand.
daily.example: Because it hurt this time, I'm sure you'll do your best next time.

daily.title: Apologizing to family
daily.description: You've been too busy with work to spend time with your family.
daily.example: Sorry I always leave you feeling lonely.

work.title: Handling a complaint
work.description: A clerk or support agent formally apologizes to a customer.
work.example: We sincerely apologize for causing you any discomfort.

work.title: News interview
work.description: A disaster survivor describes what happened to them.
work.example: The night of the earthquake was truly terrifying.

etymology: 「思い」 is the noun form of the verb 「思う」 and means “feeling, emotion”. 「思いをする」 literally means “to do a feeling”, where 「する」 means “to experience”, just like 「経験をする」 and 「苦労をする」.

similar.title: 〜羽目になる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both describe running into something unpleasant. 「〜羽目になる」 stresses the result, “ending up in a situation” (「謝る羽目になった」), while 「〜思いをする」 stresses the feeling the person tasted (「恥ずかしい思いをした」).

similar.title: 〜ような気がする
similar.explanation: Both relate to “feelings”, but 「〜ような気がする」 means “I have a feeling that ...” and expresses a vague impression or guess; 「〜思いをする」 means really going through a feeling. For “a feeling comes over me”, 「〜思いがする」 is the closer match.

similar.title: 〜と思いきや／〜かと思いきや
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built on the verb 「思う」. 「思いきや」 means “I thought ..., but (surprise)”, a letdown of expectations; the 「思い」 in 「思いをする」 is a noun meaning “feeling”. The meanings differ, only the etymology is shared.

formation: 「思い」 is a noun made from the stem of the verb 「思う」 and refers to what you feel inside; the adjective before it says which feeling. 「を」 makes that feeling the object, and 「する」 here means “to go through, experience”, the same 「する」 as in 「苦労をする」 and 「経験をする」. Put together, it is “to fully live through a certain feeling”, which is why it stresses personal experience and is mostly used in the past tense. Because 「思い」 is a noun, it needs a modifier to say which feeling it is. Replacing 「する」 with the causative 「させる」 gives “make someone else go through this feeling”, which is why it is common in apologies.

meaning: Added to a verb, it means you meant to do something but missed the chance, or you did it badly and made a mistake.
connection: Verb ます-stem + 損なう / 損ねる / 損じる

senses.label: Miss, fail to do
senses.meaning: You intended to do something, but for some reason you couldn't and missed your chance. It carries a sense of regret. Both 「損ねる」 and 「損なう」 are common; 「損ねる」 is a little more casual.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + 損ねる / 損なう (common: 見損ねる・聞き損ねる・言い損ねる・乗り損ねる・買い損ねる)
examples: I overslept and missed my usual bus.
I was so busy that I missed the movie everyone's talking about.
He went back to his country before I got a chance to thank him.

senses.label: Do it wrong, botch
senses.meaning: The action is done badly or goes wrong. Fixed words like 「書き損じる」 and 「打ち損じる」 use 「損じる」, which is more formal. The noun 「書き損じ」 means a spoiled sheet of paper.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + 損じる (common: 書き損じる・打ち損じる・仕損じる)
examples: I made a mistake filling in an important document, so I got a new form.
Haste makes waste.

senses.label: Almost, but not quite
senses.meaning: 「死に損なう」 means “to fail to die, to survive when you should have died”. From this comes the insult 「死に損ない」 (“old so-and-so who won't die”). 「見損なう」 can also mean “to misjudge someone”: 「見損なったよ」 means “I was wrong about you”.
senses.connection: Set phrases such as 死に損なう / 見損なう
examples: I can't believe you'd do something like that. I was wrong about you.
My grandfather, who barely survived the war, often told us to value our lives.

notes: 「見損なう」 has two meanings: “miss seeing something” and “misjudge a person”. Saying 「見損なったよ」 to someone means “I misjudged you, I'm very disappointed”, which is extremely strong, so don't use it casually.
「死に損ない」 is a very nasty insult (“you old good-for-nothing who won't die”). Never use it as a joke.
As a standalone verb it means “to harm”: 「部長の機嫌を損ねた」 is “I put the department head in a bad mood” and 「健康を損なう」 is “damage one's health”, unrelated to “missing” or “failing to do”.
It attaches to the ます-stem, and the two conjugate differently: ○「乗り損ねた」 (ichidan), ○「乗り損なった」 (godan); ✕「乗る損ねた」, ✕「乗り損なねた」.

daily.title: Binge-watching
daily.description: A friend asks if you saw last night's show.
daily.example: I forgot to record yesterday's finale, so I missed it.

daily.title: Sold out
daily.description: You complain to a friend that you couldn't get a limited item.
daily.example: I missed out on the limited-edition sneakers again.

daily.title: In a novel
daily.description: A character speaks to someone who betrayed them.
daily.example: I trusted you. I was wrong about you.

work.title: Missed it in a meeting
work.description: Checking with a coworker about something you didn't catch.
work.example: Sorry, I didn't catch the schedule you just mentioned.

work.title: Sports news
work.description: A commentator talks about a missed opportunity.
work.example: They blew a golden chance and couldn't score.

etymology: 「損なう」 originally means “to damage, to harm”, and 「損ねる」 is an ichidan verb with the same meaning. As helper verbs after another verb, they shift from “to spoil the action” to “to fail to do it, to botch it”. 「損じる」 is the Sino-Japanese word 「損」 + 「じる（ずる）」 and appears mostly in writing and proverbs.

similar.title: 〜そびれる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both say you missed the chance to do something. 「〜そびれる」 only means “missed it / didn't get around to it” (「言いそびれる」「寝そびれる」) and is milder; 「〜損なう／損ねる」 can also mean “botched it, got it wrong” (「書き損じる」).

similar.title: 〜ずじまい
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean something didn't get done. 「〜ずじまい」 stresses that it never happened right up to the end and the matter is over (「会えずじまいだった」); 「〜損ねる」 usually refers to missing one chance or one failed attempt.

formation: The ます-stem of the first verb expresses the action, and 「損なう」 (basic meaning “to damage, spoil”) follows as an auxiliary verb: “spoil this action”. An action can be spoiled in two ways: it never happens at all (「乗り損ねる」: miss the train), or it happens but goes wrong (「書き損じる」: write it incorrectly). 「損ねる」 is an ichidan verb with the same meaning as 「損なう」 and is more common in speech; 「損じる」 is the Sino-Japanese 「損」 plus 「じる」 and keeps a literary, proverbial flavor (「急いては事を仕損じる」). 「死に損なう」 literally means “fail to die”, and 「見損なう」 extends from “fail to see properly” to “misjudge a person”.

meaning: 「〜たことにする」 means treating something that didn't happen as if it did (pretending). 「〜たことになる」 means that, by reasoning or calculation, it counts as or equals something.
connection: Verb た-form / なかった-form + ことにする / ことになる

senses.label: Treat it as if ...
senses.meaning: The speaker deliberately treats something as true when it isn't. A common phrase is 「聞かなかったことにする」 (I'll pretend I didn't hear that). 「〜ことにしておく」 means “let's just leave it at that for now”. It suggests covering up or bending the rules.
senses.connection: Verb た-form / なかった-form + ことにする / ことにしておく
examples: I'll pretend I didn't hear what you just said.
Please consider this matter as if it never happened.
For now, let's just say I paid.

senses.label: Counts as, amounts to
senses.meaning: Based on facts, calculation or rules, it works out that “this means ...”. It is an objective conclusion. Often used with 「これで」, 「つまり」 or 「〜すると」.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + ことになる / ことになります
examples: With this, I've now visited three countries.
If you stay silent, it means you've accepted his opinion.
If you leave partway through, it doesn't count as attending.

notes: Whether it attaches to the た-form or the dictionary form changes the meaning completely: 「行くことにする」 is “decide to go”, but 「行ったことにする」 is “treat it as if I went”; 「行くことになる」 is “it's been decided that I'll go”, but 「行ったことになる」 is “it counts as having gone”.
「〜たことにする」 has a flavor of “covering up the facts” or “making allowances”. At work, 「このミスはなかったことにしましょう」 can be taken as concealment or falsification, so be careful in formal settings.
「〜たことにする」 is a deliberate stipulation, while 「〜たことになる」 is a conclusion derived from the facts; they are not interchangeable: ✕「計算すると、三割引きしたことにする」→ ○「三割引きしたことになる」.

daily.title: Keeping a secret
daily.description: You accidentally overheard a friend's secret.
daily.example: Don't worry, I'll act like I didn't hear it.

daily.title: Calculating distance
daily.description: After a run, you check how far you went on your phone.
daily.example: One lap is five kilometers, so that means I ran fifteen kilometers today.

daily.title: Calling off a promise
daily.description: Talking with a friend about canceling an earlier promise.
daily.example: Let's forget we ever made that promise.

work.title: Explaining the rules
work.description: HR explains the attendance policy.
work.example: If you arrive after nine, you will be counted as late.

work.title: Financial figures
work.description: Working out numbers in a sales report.
work.example: In other words, sales grew by twenty percent over last year.

etymology: It combines the abstract noun 「こと」 with 「にする」 (make it into) or 「になる」 (become). 「〜たこと」 packages a completed event as a whole. 「にする」 means someone deliberately decides it is so, while 「になる」 means the conclusion follows naturally.

similar.title: 〜ことにする
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are 「こと＋にする」. 「〜ことにする」 follows the dictionary form and means you decide to do something in the future (「留学することにした」); 「〜たことにする」 follows the た-form and means treating something that didn't happen as if it did.

similar.title: 〜ことになる
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are 「こと＋になる」. 「〜ることになる」 means something is decided or will turn out a certain way; 「〜たことになる」 means “is equivalent to having ..., counts as ...” by calculation or rule.

similar.title: 〜たつもり
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are “treat it as if done”. 「〜たつもり」 is imagining it in your own mind, often as self-consolation (「旅行したつもりで貯金する」); 「〜たことにする」 is handling the matter outwardly as an established fact.

similar.title: 〜ふりをする
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both involve “pretending”. 「〜ふりをする」 means putting on an act for others (「寝たふりをする」); 「〜たことにする」 means treating something as having happened in your handling or records, with no need to act it out.

formation: 「た」 fixes the event as “already happened”; the formal noun 「こと」 packages that situation as one “thing”; 「に」 marks the result of change. 「する」 is a person deliberately “making it so”, while 「なる」 is something naturally “becoming so”. So 「〜たことにする」 is deliberately settling on “it has happened”, “let's say that ...”, even if it didn't actually happen; 「〜たことになる」 is something becoming “already happened” by deduction from the facts, “amounts to, counts as”. The structure is identical to 「〜ることにする／なる」; the た-form just swaps the content for “an accomplished fact”, so the meaning shifts from “decide to do in the future” to “regard as done”.

meaning: A hypothetical contrary to fact: “if ..., it would have ...” (but it didn't actually happen).
connection: 〜たら / 〜ば / 〜なら + verb dictionary form / た-form + ところだ (ところだった)

senses.label: If ..., would have ...
senses.meaning: You imagine a condition that is contrary to fact and say what would have happened. In reality, it didn't. It often carries relief or regret. The first clause is usually 「〜ていたら」, 「〜なかったら」 or 「〜ば」.
senses.connection: 〜たら / 〜ていたら / 〜ば + verb dictionary form + ところだ (ところだった)
examples: If you hadn't stopped me, I would have been badly hurt.
If I'd been five minutes later, I would have missed my flight.
Without a map, I would have gotten lost.

senses.label: Normally, I would ...
senses.meaning: 「本来なら」, 「普通なら」 or 「いつもなら」 + 「〜ところだ（が）」 means “normally this is what would happen, but this time is different”. In business, 「本来ならこちらから伺うところですが」 is a common polite apology.
senses.connection: 本来なら / 普通なら / いつもなら + verb dictionary form + ところだ (が / けれど)
examples: I should properly visit you in person, but please excuse me for contacting you by email.
Normally I'd be angry, but I'll let it go this time.

senses.label: Past counterfactual
senses.meaning: Both parts refer to the past, contrary to fact: “if I had ..., I would have ...”. The second part uses 「〜たところだ」 and sounds more like looking back.
senses.connection: 〜ていたら + verb た-form + ところだ
examples: If I had left a little earlier, I would have made it in time.

notes: The result in the second clause did not actually happen: 「君がいなかったら、死ぬところだった」 means “I almost died (but didn't)”. Don't read it as something that really happened.
In 「家に帰ったら、母が出かけるところだった」, 「たら」 means “when I got home, I found ...” and 「ところだった」 means “(she) was just about to go out”. This is not a counterfactual.
The business phrase 「本来ならこちらから伺うところですが」 can only be used for something your own side should have done, followed by an apology; ✕「本来ならお客様が来るところですが」 sounds like blaming the other person.

daily.title: Thanking a friend
daily.description: A friend reminded you to bring an umbrella, and then it poured.
daily.example: If I hadn't brought an umbrella, I would have gotten soaked.

daily.title: A close call
daily.description: Telling your family about a near accident.
daily.example: If I had braked a moment later, I would have caused an accident.

daily.title: Letting it go
daily.description: Going easy on a child who misbehaved.
daily.example: Normally I'd scold you, but today is special.

work.title: Business email
work.description: Apologizing for emailing instead of visiting in person.
work.example: I should properly visit you to greet you in person, but please allow me to do so by email instead.

work.title: Reviewing a mistake
work.description: Explaining to your boss that you caught a problem in time.
work.example: If I hadn't checked, I would have submitted the wrong figures.

etymology: 「ところ」 originally means “place” and extends to a “stage” or “situation” in time. 「〜ところだ」 means “to be at the point of ...”. Combined with 「〜たら／〜ば」, it means “under that condition, you would have been at the point of ...”, which gives the contrary-to-fact meaning.

similar.title: 〜ところだった
similar.explanation: Same origin and also close in meaning. 「〜ところだった」 alone already means “almost ...”; 「〜たら〜ところだ（った）」 states the counterfactual condition explicitly, and can also use the present form 「ところだ」 for “by rights I should ...”.

similar.title: 〜ば〜のに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are counterfactual conditions. 「〜ば〜のに」 stresses regret or dissatisfaction, “if only ..., but unfortunately ...”; 「〜たら〜ところだった」 stresses “the outcome that would have occurred” and often carries relief.

similar.title: 〜ものを
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can express “should have ..., but didn't”. 「〜ものを」 carries strong regret or reproach (「言ってくれればよかったものを」); 「〜たら〜ところだ」 is more neutral and just states the situation that would have occurred under the condition.

similar.title: 〜ところを（contrast: should have … but）
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「ところ」 for “situation”. 「本来なら〜ところを」 is followed by what was actually done (「お忙しいところを」), while 「本来なら〜ところだ（が）」 first states at the end of the sentence what should have been, then turns around.

formation: The first half, 「〜たら／〜ば」, sets up a hypothetical condition. 「ところ」 literally means “place”; used for time it means “moment, critical point”, and dictionary form + 「ところだ」 means “be at the point of just about to ...”. Place this “about to happen” moment after a counterfactual condition, and it becomes “under that condition, things had reached the point of ...”. Because the condition is hypothetical, the result didn't actually happen, which produces the relief or regret of “almost ...”. 「本来なら〜ところだ」 works the same way: under the condition “by normal reasoning”, you would be in that situation, implying that this time is an exception.

meaning: A warning: if something bad happens, it's not my problem. You'll have only yourself to blame.
connection: Verb te-form + も知らない (知らないよ / 知らないからね)

senses.label: You'll be on your own
senses.meaning: Warns the listener that if they keep this up, something bad will happen, and the speaker won't take responsibility. It sounds strong and is used with close friends, family or people younger than you. It often ends with 「よ」, 「ぞ」 or 「からね」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + も知らない (よ / ぞ / から)
examples: If you stay up this late, don't blame me if you can't get up tomorrow.
If you don't leave soon, it's not my problem if you're late.
Don't come crying to me if you get reported to the teacher.

senses.label: I give up on you
senses.meaning: Shows you're giving up on someone who won't listen, or speaking out of frustration: “Do what you want, just don't come to me if it goes wrong.” The set phrase 「どうなっても知らない」 is common.
senses.connection: どうなっても知らない / 〜たって知らない
examples: Fine, do whatever you want. I don't care what happens.
Don't come crying to me later.

notes: It has a strong tone with blame and a threat, and must never be said to a superior, client or elder. To warn a superior, use a softer line such as 「〜と、間に合わないかもしれません」.
「知らない」 here means “it's no concern of mine”, not “I don't know”: 「遅れても知らないよ」 is “if you're late, don't come to me”.
It differs from 「〜てもかまわない」 by just one word, yet the attitude is opposite: 「遅れてもかまわない」 is “it's fine to be late”, while 「遅れても知らない」 is “if you're late, that's on you”.

daily.title: Nagging about homework
daily.description: A mother warns her child who keeps playing.
daily.example: If you don't do your homework, don't blame me when your teacher gets mad.

daily.title: Warning a friend
daily.description: Your friend is about to go out without an umbrella.
daily.example: You're not taking an umbrella? Don't blame me if you get caught in the rain.

daily.title: In an argument
daily.description: Snapping at someone you can't convince.
daily.example: Do whatever you want. Don't come to me if you regret it later.

work.title: Coworker reminder
work.description: Close coworkers half-jokingly remind each other of a deadline.
work.example: The deadline's tomorrow, you know. Not my problem if you don't make it.

etymology: 「〜ても」 is a concession: “even if ...”. 「知らない」 here means “it's none of my concern, I won't deal with it”. Together it means “even if ... happens, I'm staying out of it”, which became a fixed warning.

similar.title: 〜ても（even if）
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜ても知らない」 is the concessive 「〜ても」 plus 「知らない」. A plain 「〜ても」 can be followed by any outcome (「雨が降っても行く」), while 「〜ても知らない」 is always followed by 「知らない」 and is used specifically to warn.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うものなら
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both warn “if you do ..., there will be serious consequences”. 「〜ようものなら」 focuses on how bad the consequence is (「遅刻しようものなら、首になる」); 「〜ても知らない」 focuses on the speaker washing their hands of responsibility.

similar.title: 〜ては・〜では（bad result）
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both say “that would be bad”. 「〜ては」 points out the bad result fairly objectively (「そんなに食べては太るよ」); 「〜ても知らない」 carries the speaker's emotion and is a huffy kind of warning.

formation: 「〜ても」 is the concessive “even if ...”, with the bad outcome the other person may bring about placed before it; 「知らない」 originally means “don't know”, and here it extends to “it's not my business, I won't deal with it” (like 「そんなこと知るか」). Together: “even if ... happens, I won't care”. The concessive lays out the bad result as a foreseeable possibility, and the negative 「知らない」 pushes the responsibility back onto the listener, which makes it a warning. 「よ／ぞ／からね」 is often added at the end to throw the line directly at the listener, so the tone is harsh and it is only used with close friends or juniors.

title: 〜という (every / emphasizing numbers)
meaning: 「NというN」 stresses that every single one in a group is included: “every last ..., without exception”. 「number + という」 stresses how large a number is.
connection: Noun + という + the same noun / number word + という + noun

senses.label: Every single ...
senses.meaning: The same noun is repeated with 「という」 in between to mean “every ..., all ...”, with no exceptions. It is often followed by 「すべて」, 「みな」 or 「どこも」. Mostly used in writing and descriptions.
senses.connection: Noun + という + the same noun (common: 家という家・窓という窓・店という店・人という人)
examples: The typhoon damaged every single house in the village.
I opened every window to air out the room.
Every bone in my body hurts.

senses.label: As many as ...
senses.meaning: After number words like 「何百」, 「何千」, 「何万」 or 「数千」, it stresses a very large number: “hundreds of”, “tens of thousands of”. It sounds amazed.
senses.connection: 何十 / 何百 / 何千 / 何万 / 数万 etc. + という + noun
examples: Tens of thousands of people gathered at the venue.
I get hundreds of emails every day.

notes: 「NというN」 must repeat the same noun: ✕「家という建物」→ ○「家という家」.
For quantity, it normally attaches to indefinite quantity words such as 「何百・何千・数万」; for a specific number, 「三万人もの人」 is more common, and ✕「三万という人が来た」 sounds unnatural.
Don't confuse it with the naming 「〜という」: 「田中という人」 is “a person called Tanaka”, not “all people”.

daily.title: In a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a whole town coming alive.
daily.example: That night, every shop in town lit up.

daily.title: Big cleanup
daily.description: Telling your family how thoroughly you cleaned.
daily.example: I tidied up every single drawer.

daily.title: At a concert
daily.description: Telling a friend how packed it was.
daily.example: Tens of thousands of fans had packed into the dome.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting how severe the damage is.
work.example: The earthquake cut off every road.

work.title: Market analysis
work.description: Explaining how popular a product is.
work.example: Thousands of orders poured in on the first day of sales.

etymology: 「という」 comes from the quoting particle 「と」 + 「言う」 and is used for definitions and names. 「NというN」 literally means “an N called N”, that is, “anything that can be called N”, which gives the meaning “all”. With numbers, it adds an exaggerated sense of “as many as ...”.

similar.title: 〜という〜（all …）
similar.explanation: Same meaning: both use 「NというN」 for “all ...” (「窓という窓」). This entry also covers the quantity-emphasizing use like 「何万という人」.

similar.title: 〜という〜（emphasizing quantity）
similar.explanation: Same meaning: it covers only the quantity-emphasizing use like 「何百という人」. In 「NというN」 of this entry it is the noun that is repeated, to mean “all”, so the repeated element differs between the two.

similar.title: 〜という（called）
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from 「と＋言う」. 「〜という」 originally means a name or label (「山田という人」); this grammar point borrows the sense of “worthy of the name ...” to stress “all” or a large quantity.

similar.title: 〜に至るまで
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both stress wide range with no exceptions. 「〜に至るまで」 names the far end of a range (「子どもから老人に至るまで」); 「NというN」 repeats the same noun to vividly mean “every single one”.

formation: 「という」 is made of the quoting 「と」 plus 「言う」 and originally means “called ...”. 「家という家」 literally is “the houses called ‘houses’”, i.e. “everything that deserves the name ‘house’”: using the name to enclose every member of the whole category, so it means “all ...”. After a quantity word such as 「何万」, 「という」 presents the number as a so-called figure, with a tone of surprise, “as many as that”. Both uses exploit the naming and quoting function of 「という」 to emphasize range or quantity.

meaning: Brings up a special condition or feature to stress “and on top of that ...”, leading to a natural result or comment.
connection: Noun / adjective / verb plain form + ときている

senses.label: And on top of that
senses.meaning: Adds another standout condition to one already mentioned: “on top of that ...”. The next part is the natural result. Often used with 「そのうえ」, 「おまけに」 or 「しかも」. It carries the speaker's admiration or judgment.
senses.connection: Noun / い-adjective / な-adjective stem + ときている (から / ので)
examples: This place is cheap and delicious, so there's always a line.
He's smart, and on top of that, he's rich.

senses.label: And to make it worse
senses.meaning: Used for negative situations: “it's already ..., and on top of that ...”, stressing that things go from bad to worse. It sounds dissatisfied or resigned.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective plain form + ときている
examples: There's tons of work, and the pay is low on top of that. No wonder I want to quit.
The road is narrow, and there's lots of traffic too.

notes: It carries the speaker's subjective judgment (exclamation, sarcasm, dissatisfaction), so using it to comment on a superior or a client themselves comes across as careless and rude.

「〜ときている」 comes at the end of the sentence to add a striking condition; 「〜ときたら」 comes at the start to raise a topic and then criticize it. Position and use differ: ✕「うちの子ときている、勉強しない」→ ○「うちの子ときたら、勉強しない」.
In 「友達と来ている」 (“have come with a friend”), 「と」 means “with” and 「来ている」 is literal “come”; this is not the grammar point.

daily.title: Recommending a restaurant
daily.description: Recommending a place to a friend.
daily.example: It's close to the station, and the portions are big too. It's the best.

daily.title: Complaining about your apartment
daily.description: Griping to a friend about where you live.
daily.example: My room is tiny, and it doesn't get much sun either.

daily.title: Praising someone
daily.description: Praising an impressive acquaintance.
daily.example: She's beautiful, and she's a great cook on top of that.

work.title: Why it sells
work.description: Explaining in a meeting why a product is a hit.
work.example: It's reasonably priced and well designed, so naturally it sells.

work.title: Complaining about a project
work.description: Coworkers privately grumbling about project conditions.
work.example: The budget is tiny, and the deadline is next week to boot.

etymology: It comes from the quoting particle 「と」 + the ている-form of 「来る」. 「と来る」 originally meant “(the topic or situation) comes to this point”. It shares its origin with 「〜ときたら」 and 「〜ときたもんだ」, and singles out a feature for emphasis.

similar.title: 〜ときたら
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built from 「と＋来る」. 「〜ときたら」 raises a person or thing as the topic and criticizes it (「うちの夫ときたら」); 「〜ときている」 adds a striking condition at the end of the sentence and leads to the consequence.

similar.title: 〜上(に)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “on top of that ...”. 「〜上に」 simply adds information in the same direction, objectively; 「〜ときている」 carries the exclamation or complaint of “and on top of that ...”, so its subjective color is strong.

similar.title: 〜ばかりか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are cumulative. 「〜ばかりか」 means “not only ... but also ...” and stresses progression (「遅刻したばかりか、宿題も忘れた」); 「〜ときている」 pulls out the last condition for exclamation and then leads to the conclusion.

similar.title: 〜とあって／〜とあっては
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both present a special circumstance and then give the result. 「〜とあって」 is mostly used in news reports, explaining the reason objectively; 「〜ときている」 is more colloquial and carries the speaker's subjective feelings.

formation: The quoting particle 「と」 raises the preceding thing or feature as the “topic”; 「来る」 here does not mean “come” but “(a topic, a situation) comes up, turns up”, so 「〜と来る」 is “when it comes to ..., there it is”; 「ている」 shows the situation is now laid out before you and continues. Together: “and on top of that there's also ...”, pulling out one striking condition, which carries exclamation or dissatisfaction and naturally leads to the “no wonder ...” consequence. Also built from 「と＋来る」 are 「〜ときたら」 and 「〜ときたもんだ」.

meaning: As soon as someone sees (judges) a certain situation, they act right away.
connection: Verb / adjective plain form, noun + と見るや (否や) / と見ると

senses.label: The moment they see ...
senses.meaning: Right after seeing or judging a situation, someone acts immediately. It stresses quick judgment and fast reaction. Mostly used to describe other people's actions. It is written style, common in novels and news.
senses.connection: Plain form + と見るや / と見るや否や
examples: The moment the criminal saw the police officer approaching, he ran off.
The moment they saw their opponent weakening, they launched an all-out attack.
As soon as he saw the stock price start to fall, he sold all his shares.

senses.label: Once they judge ...
senses.meaning: 「〜と見ると」 is a bit softer: “once (someone) judges that ..., they ...”. It can also describe the speaker's own actions and is fine in both writing and speech.
senses.connection: Plain form + と見ると / とみると
examples: Once he saw he couldn't win, he immediately changed tactics.
The moment the cat sees someone coming, it darts off and hides.

notes: The second clause is an action that actually took place, usually in the past tense; commands, volition and requests cannot follow: ✕「敵が来たと見るや、逃げろ」→ ○「敵が来たと見るや、彼らは逃げ出した」.
「見る」 here means “judge, make out”, and what comes before can be the content of the judgment (「勝てないと見るや」); don't read it as “as soon as (they) saw”.
It is literary and mostly used to describe other people's quick reactions; in everyday conversation 「〜とわかると、すぐ…」 sounds more natural.

daily.title: Watching sports
daily.description: Commenting on a great moment in a game.
daily.example: The moment he saw his chance, he sprinted straight to the goal.

daily.title: In a novel
daily.description: Describing a character who switches sides easily.
daily.example: As soon as he saw things turning against him, he went over to the other side.

work.title: Financial news
work.description: Reporting how investors reacted to the market.
work.example: As soon as investors judged that the yen would keep weakening, they started buying dollars.

work.title: Business commentary
work.description: Commenting on a company's sharp decision.
work.example: The moment the company saw the market would grow, it launched a new product.

etymology: 「と見る」 means “to judge that ...”. 「や」 is a classical conjunctive particle meaning “as soon as” (the same 「や」 as in 「や否や」). Because it keeps this classical flavor, the expression sounds formal and tight.

similar.title: 〜や否や／〜や
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use the classical 「や」 for “as soon as ...”. 「〜や否や」 attaches directly to an action (「ドアが開くや否や」) and means two actions follow immediately; 「〜と見るや」 stresses first “reading the situation” and then acting quickly.

similar.title: 〜が早いか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean something follows immediately. 「〜が早いか」 stresses two actions being almost simultaneous (「ベルが鳴るが早いか」); 「〜と見るや」 focuses on adapting on the spot after the judgment.

similar.title: 〜なり（as soon as）
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are “as soon as ...”. After 「〜なり」 there is usually an unexpected action (「顔を見るなり泣き出した」); after 「〜と見るや」 is the subject's deliberate response.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean something happens right after. After 「〜たとたん」 the second clause is mostly an unexpected change, and it works in both speech and writing; after 「〜と見るや」 the second clause is the subject's active move, with a strongly literary flavor.

formation: 「と」 is the quoting particle, presenting the content of the judgment; 「見る」 here means “regard as, judge to be” (the same 「見る」 as in 「〜と見られる」); 「や」 is a classical conjunctive particle meaning “as soon as ...”, the same 「や」 as in 「や否や」. Put together: “as soon as one judges it to be ..., then ...”. Because the core is the act of judging in 「と見る」, it stresses “reading the situation and reacting at once”, not merely two actions in succession. The classical 「や」 makes the whole phrase tight and literary; swapping 「や」 for the colloquial conditional 「と」 gives the milder, more general 「〜と見ると」.

meaning: Written style. Means something is generally thought to be, regarded as, or officially defined as something.
connection: Noun / plain form + とされる (とされた / とされ)

senses.label: Is regarded as
senses.meaning: States a widely held view of society or experts objectively, without giving the speaker's own opinion. More formal than 「〜と言われる」. Common in news, academic papers and explanations.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + とされる
examples: This temple is considered the oldest wooden building in Japan.
Lack of sleep is considered one of the causes of obesity.
Mt. Fuji has been regarded as a sacred mountain since ancient times.

senses.label: Is ruled as
senses.meaning: Means something is defined as a certain status by law, rules or a decision. Common in legal and official documents.
senses.connection: Noun + とされる (common: 無効とされる・違法とされる・対象とされる)
examples: Applications submitted after the deadline will be considered invalid.
That act was declared illegal by law.

senses.label: Is said to have
senses.meaning: After a verb in the た-form, it means “it is said that ...”. Mostly used for history and legends, where the truth is uncertain.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + とされる
examples: I visited a temple said to have been founded by Kūkai.

notes: 「〜とされる」 only relays what society or an authority has determined and doesn't express your own opinion: ✕「私は、この方法が最善とされる」→ ○「私は、この方法が最善だと考える」.
Active and passive take different subjects: ○「政府はこの地域を危険区域とした」／○「この地域は危険区域とされた」; ✕「政府はこの地域を危険区域とされた」.
「される」 can also be honorific: 「先生はこの問題を研究テーマとされている」 means “the professor takes this problem as a research theme”, not “is considered”, so judge by the subject.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A health news story presents research findings.
daily.example: Walking 10,000 steps a day is considered ideal.

daily.title: Sightseeing
daily.description: A tour guide introduces a famous spot.
daily.example: This shrine is said to be home to the god of love.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Citing views from earlier research.
work.example: Until now, this phenomenon has been attributed to climate change.

work.title: Contract clause
work.description: Setting out what happens in case of a breach.
work.example: If this contract is breached, the contract shall be deemed terminated.

etymology: It is made of the quoting particle 「と」 + the passive 「される」 of 「する」 (to regard as, to treat as). 「AをBとする」 means “to treat A as B”. In the passive, it becomes “A is treated as B”, expressing a general or official judgment.

similar.title: 〜とされている
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「ている」 form of the same structure. 「〜とされている」 stresses that this determination is still widely held now; 「〜とされる」 is more concise and often used as a modifier (「原因とされる物質」).

similar.title: 〜と言われている
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both relay other people's views. 「〜と言われている」 is “people say”, more colloquial, and the source needn't be authoritative; 「〜とされる」 is more formal and mostly refers to determinations by experts or authorities.

similar.title: 〜ものと思われる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are written, objective expressions. 「〜ものと思われる」 is an inference drawn from the circumstances (「事故の原因は寝不足によるものと思われる」); 「〜とされる」 relays an existing determination or rule.

similar.title: 〜を〜とする・〜を〜として
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜とされる」 is the passive of 「AをBとする」. 「AをBとする」 states who designates A as B (「会議の目的を情報共有とする」); in 「AはBとされる」 the one who decides is hidden, which sounds objective.

formation: 「と」 is the quoting particle that marks the content of the determination; 「する」 in 「AをBとする」 means “designate A as B, regard as B”. Turning 「する」 into the passive 「される」 changes the subject from “the person who makes the determination” to “the thing being determined”, i.e. “A is designated as B”. With the decider hidden, the sentence only states that “society, an authority, regards it so”, which naturally sounds objective and noncommittal. What is determined can be a view (“is regarded as”), a rule (“is set as”) or a tradition (“is said to be”); all three senses come from the same “being determined” structure.

meaning: 「AともBとも言わない」 means not saying either A or B, refusing to give a clear answer. 「AともBともつかない」 means you can't tell whether it's A or B.
connection: Noun / verb plain form + とも + noun / verb plain form + とも + 言わない / つかない etc.

senses.label: No clear answer
senses.meaning: In 「AともBとも言わない」, A and B are usually opposites (「行く／行かない」, 「はい／いいえ」). It means the other person won't give a clear answer, often with impatience or annoyance. The set phrase 「うんともすんとも言わない」 means “not a peep”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + とも + verb ない-form + とも言わない / 答えない
examples: He didn't say whether he'd go or not.
I sent an email, but I haven't heard a peep back.
The manager didn't say whether he was for or against it.

senses.label: Can't tell which
senses.meaning: 「AともBともつかない」 means something is somewhere between A and B, and it's hard to tell which. Mostly used to describe voices, expressions and attitudes. Rather literary.
senses.connection: Noun + とも + noun + ともつかない (ともつかぬ)
examples: She let out a sound that was somewhere between laughing and crying.
He said it in a tone where I couldn't tell if he was joking or serious.

senses.label: Could be called A or B
senses.meaning: 「AともBとも言える」 means that, depending on how you look at it, it could be called A or B. Common in commentary and analysis.
senses.connection: Noun + とも + noun + とも言える
examples: That personality trait could be called a strength or a weakness.

notes: A and B must be a pair or opposites: ✕「行くとも行くとも言わない」→ ○「行くとも行かないとも言わない」.
The ending decides the meaning: 「AともBとも言えない／言わない」 is “says neither”, while 「AともBとも言える」 is “can be called either”; flipping affirmative and negative reverses the meaning.
「うんともすんとも言わない」 carries clear dissatisfaction; saying 「部長はうんともすんとも言わない」 about a boss or client sounds disrespectful, so in formal settings say 「まだお返事をいただいていません」.
The 「とも」 in 「二人とも」 and 「両方とも」 means “both”; it is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Inviting a friend
daily.description: A friend still hasn't answered your party invitation.
daily.example: He hasn't said whether he's coming or not.

daily.title: In a novel
daily.description: Describing a character's complicated expression.
daily.example: His face showed something between anger and sadness.

work.title: Negotiation report
work.description: Telling your boss how the client responded.
work.example: They didn't say clearly whether they would sign the contract or not.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: Analyzing both sides of a policy.
work.example: This reform could be called either a success or a failure.

etymology: 「とも」 is the quoting particle 「と」 + the particle 「も」. 「Aとも言わない」 means “doesn't even say A”. Putting two options side by side as 「AともBとも」 gives “doesn't say A or B”, which means not committing to either.

similar.title: 〜のやら〜のやら
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean you can't tell whether it is A or B. 「〜のやら〜のやら」 is the speaker's own bewilderment, “I can't tell if ... or ...” (「喜んでいるのやら怒っているのやら」); 「〜とも〜ともつかない」 describes how the thing itself is hard to categorize.

similar.title: 〜というか〜というか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both set two expressions side by side. 「〜というか〜というか」 is the speaker weighing how to put it (「大胆というか無謀というか」); 「〜とも〜ともつかない」 says neither option is certain.

similar.title: 〜ともなく／〜ともなしに
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built from 「と＋も」. 「〜ともなく」 means doing something without a clear intention (「見るともなく見る」); 「〜とも〜とも」 lines up two options and says neither is clear.

formation: 「とも」 is the quoting particle 「と」 plus the emphatic particle 「も」. 「と」 treats A and B as what is said or judged, and 「も」 gives the parallel “A too, B too”. Followed by the negative 「言わない」, it is “says neither A nor B”, i.e. takes no stance; followed by 「つかない」 (cannot classify, tell apart), it is “can't be filed as A, can't be filed as B”, i.e. hard to tell; followed by 「言える」, it is “can say A, can say B”. So the actual meaning is decided by the final verb, and 「AともBとも」 only sets the two options side by side.

meaning: Means “for someone like ... (who shouldn't slip up) to actually ...”. Expresses self-blame or surprise at an unexpected mistake.
connection: Noun referring to a person + としたことが

senses.label: Self-blame: How could I ...
senses.meaning: Usually 「私としたことが」: “I normally wouldn't do this, but I actually made this mistake.” It sounds regretful or self-mocking. What follows is usually the mistake, or an exclamation like 「なんということだ」.
senses.connection: 私 / 僕 / 俺 + としたことが
examples: How could I have left such an important document at home?
I can't believe I made such a simple mistake.

senses.label: Surprise: even ... did that
senses.meaning: Used about others: “even someone as capable or careful as them actually ...”. Shows surprise at their mistake. Usually about someone the speaker respects.
senses.connection: Name / noun referring to a person + としたことが
examples: Who'd have thought that even our careful senior colleague would get the meeting time wrong?
Even a veteran like him failed, which is rare.

notes: Use it only for unexpected mistakes, never for good things: ✕「私としたことが、試験に合格した」.
「私としたことが」 implies “this isn't like me”; when apologizing to a superior or client, saying only this may sound like making excuses and insincere, so add a clear apology such as 「大変申し訳ございません」.
Used about others, it carries surprise and regret and affirms their usual ability; to criticize a high-ranking person for neglecting duty, use 「〜ともあろう者が」, which has a completely different tone.

daily.title: Forgot the key
daily.description: You realize after leaving home that you forgot something, and mutter to yourself.
daily.example: Oh, how could I forget to lock the door!

daily.title: A friend slips up
daily.description: A friend who is always on time is late.
daily.example: You're always so strict about time. It's rare for you to be late.

daily.title: In a mystery novel
daily.description: A detective realizes they missed a clue.
daily.example: How could I, of all people, have overlooked such a clue?

work.title: Apologizing to a client
work.description: You realize you sent the wrong materials.
work.example: I'm terribly sorry. Through my own carelessness, I sent you the wrong materials.

etymology: It is made of the quoting particle 「と」 + 「した」 (past of 「する」) + 「こと」 + 「が」. 「Aとする」 means “as A, being A”, so 「Aとしたことが」 literally means “what someone who is A did”, extended to “for A to actually ...”. It carries a sense that the act doesn't fit who they are.

similar.title: 〜ともあろう
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “someone like ..., yet ...”. 「〜ともあろう」 criticizes a person of status for doing what they shouldn't (「教師ともあろう者が」), is formal and heavy; 「〜としたことが」 is mostly self-reproach or regret, with a lighter tone.

similar.title: 〜にしては
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean it doesn't match the expected status or standard. 「〜にしては」 can praise or criticize (「初心者にしては上手だ」); 「〜としたことが」 is only for an ordinarily reliable person slipping up unexpectedly.

similar.title: 〜として
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜とした」 is the past form of 「〜とする」 (“as”). 「〜として」 is the neutral “as ...” (「代表として出席する」); 「〜としたことが」 uses “being ...” to introduce an unexpected lapse out of keeping with that role.

formation: 「と」 plus 「する」 makes 「〜とする」 (“as ..., being ...”), and here the past form 「した」 modifies the noun: 「私としたこと」 literally is “the thing done by someone who is me”. The case particle 「が」 raises this as the subject, and the predicate that should follow, such as 「信じられない」, is usually omitted, leaving only the tone of astonishment. The omitted part is exactly “an unexpected lapse not befitting the role”, so the whole phrase means “someone like me (him), and yet ...”. Since it stresses the “role”, only a person can precede it, and it is used only for mistakes that don't suit that role.

meaning: Means the gap between two things is so huge that they can't even be compared.
connection: Noun + とは比べものにならない

senses.label: Not even in the same league
senses.meaning: A and B are so far apart that there's no comparison. Usually A is far better (or greater) than B, but it can also mean A is far worse. It is strong and a bit exaggerated.
senses.connection: AはBとは比べものにならない
examples: A professional chef's cooking is in a different league from mine.
Today's smartphones are incomparably better than those of ten years ago.

senses.label: Incomparably ...
senses.meaning: 「比べものにならないほど／くらい」 works like an adverb: the degree is astonishingly high, “incomparably ...”.
senses.connection: 〜とは比べものにならないほど + adjective / verb
examples: The new house is incomparably bigger than the old one.
Tokyo has far, far more people than my town.

notes: 「AはBとは比べものにならない」 usually means A is far better than B, so check the subject: ○「私の作品は先生の作品とは比べものになりません」 is modest; swap the subjects and it becomes boasting, which is very rude.
「比べられない」 means “can't be compared (each has its merits)” and doesn't express a big gap: ✕「新しいパソコンは古いのとは比べられないほど速い」→ ○「比べものにならないほど速い」.

daily.title: Great food
daily.description: Eating ramen at a long-established shop.
daily.example: The ramen here is in a whole different league from instant noodles.

daily.title: Talking about skill
daily.description: After watching a professional game.
daily.example: The speed of the pros is nothing like amateurs.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Telling a friend how hot this summer is.
daily.example: This year's heat is way worse than last year's.

work.title: Product introduction
work.description: Presenting a new product's strengths to a client.
work.example: The new model's processing speed is vastly better than previous products.

work.title: Economic news
work.description: Reporting on how a country's economy has grown.
work.example: Today's economy is incomparably larger than thirty years ago.

etymology: 「比べもの」 is the ます-stem of 「比べる」 + 「もの」, meaning “something to compare with”. 「比べものにならない」 literally means “doesn't even become something to compare”, that is, the gap is too wide to put them side by side.

similar.title: 〜に比べて
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built on 「比べる」. 「〜に比べて」 is an ordinary comparison, “compared to ...” (「去年に比べて暑い」); 「〜とは比べものにならない」 stresses a gap so big there's no basis for comparison.

similar.title: 〜には及ばない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜には及ばない」 also means “falls short of” (「彼の実力には遠く及ばない」), with the inferior side as the subject; 「〜とは比べものにならない」 works both ways and often takes the better side as the subject.

similar.title: 〜ほど〜はない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can express an extremely high degree. 「〜ほど〜はない」 is “there is nothing more ... than ...”, stressing being number one (「母の料理ほどおいしいものはない」); 「〜とは比べものにならない」 contrasts two things and stresses a huge gap.

formation: 「比べもの」 is the stem 「比べ」 of the verb 「比べる」 plus 「もの」, meaning “something you can compare, a point of comparison”; 「〜になる」 is “become, qualify as”, so the negative 「ならない」 is “doesn't qualify”. The 「と」 in 「とは」 marks the other side of the comparison, and 「は」 adds contrast. Together: “next to B, it doesn't even qualify as something to compare”, a gap so large that putting them side by side is meaningless, hence “worlds apart”. When followed by 「ほど／くらい」, this “beyond comparison” degree is turned around to modify an adjective, meaning “astonishingly ...”.

meaning: Added to a verb, it means doing something completely and thoroughly, with nothing left over.

senses.label: Use up, ... it all
senses.meaning: Means using up, eating up or selling out all of something, with nothing left. It stresses doing it completely. Common examples: 「食べ尽くす」, 「使い尽くす」, 「売り尽くす」, 「燃やし尽くす」.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + 尽くす (食べ尽くす・使い尽くす・売り尽くす)
examples: A huge swarm of locusts devoured every crop in the fields.
I've used up all my savings.
The square was completely filled with spectators.

senses.label: Thoroughly, exhaustively
senses.meaning: Means taking an action as far as it can go, leaving nothing out. Common: 「知り尽くす」 (know inside out), 「言い尽くす」 (say everything), 「味わい尽くす」 (savor to the fullest).
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + 尽くす (知り尽くす・言い尽くす・味わい尽くす・調べ尽くす)
examples: He knows this town inside out.
Words can't fully express how moved I am.

senses.label: Stand frozen
senses.meaning: 「立ち尽くす」 is a set phrase meaning to stand still and not move because of shock, grief and so on: “to stand frozen”.
senses.connection: 立ち尽くす
examples: When she heard the news, she stood frozen on the spot.

notes: 「尽くす」 is transitive (actively use up), while 「尽きる」 is intransitive (run out by itself): ✕「お金が使い尽くした」→ ○「お金を使い尽くした」／○「お金が尽きた」.
「〜に尽くす」 means “devote oneself to ...” (「社会に尽くす」「家族に尽くす」), a different use from the auxiliary verb attached to a verb.
「知り尽くす」 is very strong; telling a client 「御社のことは知り尽くしています」 can sound exaggerated and arrogant, and in business 「よく存じております」 is more fitting.

daily.title: All-you-can-eat
daily.description: Joking with a friend at a buffet.
daily.example: Today I'm eating until I've gotten my money's worth!

daily.title: Travel tips
daily.description: Recommending a city you know well.
daily.example: Leave Kyoto to me. I'm a local, so I know it inside out.

daily.title: In a novel
daily.description: Describing the hero hearing terrible news.
daily.example: He stood frozen, stunned, in front of his burned-down house.

work.title: Store ad
work.description: A clearance sale slogan.
work.example: Everything half price until it's all sold out!

work.title: Promise to clients
work.description: Introducing the team's expertise.
work.example: Experts who know the industry inside out will answer your questions.

etymology: 「尽くす」 originally means “to exhaust, to use up”, as in 「力を尽くす」. As a helper verb after another verb, it means pushing that action to the limit with nothing left. It is the transitive partner of the intransitive 「尽きる」 (to run out, to end).

similar.title: 〜きる・〜きれない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean doing something to the end. 「〜きる」 stresses carrying one thing through from start to finish, completing it (「読みきる」「走りきる」); 「〜尽くす」 stresses using up the whole object with nothing left, or exhausting its extent, and is stronger and more literary.

similar.title: 〜抜く
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean thoroughly. 「〜抜く」 stresses overcoming difficulty and persisting to the end (「最後まで戦い抜く」) or an extreme degree (「悩み抜く」); 「〜尽くす」 stresses using up so nothing remains.

similar.title: 〜通す
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean doing to the end. 「〜通す」 stresses not giving up midway and keeping it up (「最後まで歩き通す」「嘘をつき通す」); 「〜尽くす」 stresses exhausting the whole object.

formation: The stem of the first verb expresses the action, followed by the auxiliary 「尽くす」 (basic meaning “exhaust, use up”): doing the action “until nothing is left”. When the object is a finite thing, it is “all of it ... completely” (「食べ尽くす」「売り尽くす」); when it is abstract, such as knowledge, language or feelings, it is “exhaust, thoroughly” (「知り尽くす」「言い尽くす」). 「立ち尽くす」 stretches the act of standing to its limit and extends to standing rooted to the spot. Because 「尽くす」 is transitive, it stresses the subject actively “using up”, and it pairs with the intransitive 「尽きる」 (run out naturally).

meaning: Means something is too minor to count as a certain thing: “that doesn't even count as ...”.
connection: Noun + の + うちに入らない

senses.label: Doesn't count as ...
senses.meaning: Something is too slight to belong in that category. Common form: 「〜のうちに入らない」. It suggests “that's nothing worth mentioning”, and can sound modest or dismissive.
senses.connection: Noun + の + うちに入らない (入りません)
examples: A drizzle like this doesn't count as rain.
Walking for an hour doesn't really count as exercise.
That doesn't even count as a fight.

senses.label: Does it count as ...?
senses.meaning: The question form 「〜のうちに入る？」 asks whether something qualifies, often sounding self-mocking or doubtful.
senses.connection: Noun + の + うちに入るの？ / うちに入りますか
examples: Does making cup noodles count as cooking?

notes: Said about yourself it is modest (「これくらい、苦労のうちに入りません」); said about someone else's suffering or effort it is belittling: telling a sick person 「そんなの病気のうちに入らない」 is very hurtful and rude.
After a noun, 「の」 is needed: ✕「雨うちに入らない」→ ○「雨のうちに入らない」.
It is completely different from 「〜うちに」 (while ...): 「若いうちに」 is “while you're young”; the 「うち」 in 「勝手にうちに入らないで」 is “home”.

daily.title: Being modest
daily.description: A friend praises your cooking.
daily.example: Oh no, this hardly counts as cooking.

daily.title: Talking about fitness
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about how much you exercise.
daily.example: Just walking to the station doesn't count as exercise, right?

daily.title: Talking about travel
daily.description: A friend says they've been to a country, but only changed planes there.
daily.example: If you just changed planes at the airport, that doesn't count as going there.

work.title: Talking about overtime
work.description: A veteran employee talks about how hard work used to be.
work.example: Compared to the old days, this much overtime doesn't even count as overtime.

etymology: 「うち（内）」 originally means “inside, within a range”. 「〜のうちに入る」 means “to be counted within ...”, so the negative 「入らない」 means “not within that range”, which gives “doesn't count as ...”.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい（belittling / minimum）
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both play something down as trivial. 「〜くらい」 is “a mere ...” (「これくらい平気だ」) and is often used together with this grammar point: 「一時間歩くくらい、運動のうちに入らない」. 「〜うちに入らない」 goes further and declares “it doesn't qualify as that category”.

similar.title: 〜にすぎない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both indicate a low degree. 「〜にすぎない」 is “nothing more than ...”, an objective limitation (「噂にすぎない」); 「〜うちに入らない」 is “doesn't count as ...”, denying it belongs to a category, and is more colloquial.

similar.title: 〜ほどのことではない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “not worth it, not to that extent”. 「〜ほどのことではない」 follows an action and means “not serious enough to ...” (「騒ぐほどのことではない」); 「〜うちに入らない」 follows a noun and means it doesn't qualify for that category.

similar.title: 〜うちに
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from 「うち（内）」. 「〜うちに」 applies 「うち」 to a time span, meaning “while ...”; 「〜のうちに入らない」 applies 「うち」 to a category, meaning “isn't counted within ...”.

formation: 「うち（内）」 basically means “inside, within a range”, so 「〜のうち」 is “within the range of ...”; 「に入る」 is “enter, be counted in”, and the negative 「入らない」 is “doesn't get in, isn't counted”. Together: “doesn't get inside the range of ...”, i.e. fails the standard for that category and doesn't count as ... . The speaker uses this to push the object's degree down, so it carries a tone of “not worth mentioning”. In the question form 「〜のうちに入る？」 it asks “does it qualify?”.

title: 〜わ (sentence-ending particle)
meaning: A sentence-ending particle. In feminine speech it softens a statement or exclamation. In Kansai and some other regions, both men and women use it for a light assertion.
connection: Plain form / です・ます form + わ (わよ / わね)

senses.label: Soft feminine tone
senses.meaning: Feminine speech with rising intonation. It makes opinions and impressions sound softer. Often combined as 「わよ」 or 「わね」. In modern speech it sounds a bit old-fashioned and is mostly heard from female characters in novels, TV and film.
senses.connection: Plain form + わ (わよ / わね)
examples: Oh my, what lovely flowers.
I'm coming with you too, you know.
I have no idea about that.

senses.label: Light assertion
senses.meaning: With falling intonation, it expresses the speaker's decision or impression, almost like talking to yourself. In the Kansai dialect both men and women use it often, and young men use it in standard Japanese too.
senses.connection: Plain form + わ (falling intonation)
examples: I'm tired, so I'm heading home.
That's just not possible.

senses.label: One after another
senses.meaning: 「〜わ〜わ」 repeats the same verb or lists two verbs to mean things keep happening one after another, more than expected, with surprise or exasperation. For example 「出るわ出るわ」 (they just keep coming).
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + わ + verb dictionary form + わ
examples: When I looked into it, the problems just kept coming.
It rained and the wind blew. What a terrible day.

notes: Rising 「わ」 has a strong feminine feel, and a man saying it in standard Japanese sounds feminine; falling 「わ」 can be used by anyone (「もう帰るわ」).
It belongs to casual speech between people who are close; saying 「行くわ」 or 「無理だわ」 to a superior or client sounds casual and rude, so it isn't used in business.
「〜わ〜わ」 repeats the same verb or lines up two clauses, for surprising or troublesome things happening one after another: 「出るわ出るわ」. It can't be used for a plain list.
The sentence-final particle 「わ」 must not be written 「は」; the 「は」 in 「これは」 is the topic particle.

daily.title: Watching a Japanese drama
daily.description: A female character shares her feelings.
daily.example: You're really so kind. I'm so happy.

daily.title: Saying goodbye
daily.description: A friend from Kansai says they're heading off.
daily.example: Well then, I'd better get going.

daily.title: Complaining about bad luck
daily.description: Venting to a friend about a terrible day.
daily.example: I lost my wallet, and the trains stopped. Today is the worst.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers
work.description: Casually saying goodbye to a close coworker at the end of the day.
work.example: I'm worn out today. See you.

etymology: It is generally thought to come from the binding particle 「は」, used at the end of a sentence for emphasis and later written 「わ」. From the late Edo period it became fixed in feminine speech, while the Kansai dialect kept the use for both men and women.

similar.title: 〜よ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are sentence-final particles that assert something. 「〜よ」 tells the listener information they don't know and is more direct; 「〜わ」 expresses the speaker's own feeling or decision, in a softer tone or as if talking to oneself, and the two are often combined as 「わよ」.

similar.title: 〜ね
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are sentence-final particles. 「〜ね」 seeks the listener's agreement or confirmation; 「〜わ」 is the speaker's one-sided exclamation or decision, and combined as 「わね」 it carries both exclamation and a request for agreement.

similar.title: 〜かしら
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are particles with a feminine flavor. 「〜かしら」 expresses a question or wondering to oneself (「明日晴れるかしら」); 「〜わ」 expresses exclamation or a soft assertion, and is not a question.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: Close in meaning, matching the 「〜わ〜わ」 use: both list messy things happening one after another. 「〜やら〜やら」 attaches to nouns or verbs with a flatter tone (「洗濯やら掃除やら」); 「〜わ〜わ」 attaches only to verb clauses and carries stronger surprise or exasperation.

formation: The sentence-final 「わ」 is generally thought to come from the binding particle 「は」: 「は」 originally raises and stresses an item, and placed at the end of a sentence it “presents” the whole judgment, strengthening an exclamation or assertion, and later came to be read and written 「わ」. With rising intonation, this exclamation is tossed softly to the listener, making it feminine speech; with falling intonation, it sounds more like confirmation spoken to oneself, so both men and women can use it. 「〜わ〜わ」 strings two such exclamatory short clauses together, giving the listing exclamation of “first this, then that, with no end”.
